title: IT vs OT
desc: Office networks versus industrial control systems

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security
NCSC Ireland NIS2 quick reference guide

lessons.title: IT vs OT in one minute

pages.t: IT is the office world: laptops, servers, email, Wi-Fi. OT is the machine world: hardware and software that monitors or controls physical equipment such as pumps, production lines and building systems.
g: Information technology: computers, networks and data for running a business.
Operational technology: systems that control physical processes.

pages.t: Think factories, power and water plants, oil and gas, mining, transport and building management. It was jokingly called 'IT in the non-carpeted areas'. A PLC or a SCADA system is typical OT.
g: A rugged industrial computer that controls a machine or process.
Software that supervises many machines and sites from one control room.

pages.t: OT used to be isolated from the office network. Today OT is increasingly connected to IT for monitoring and management. This is called IT/OT convergence, and it is why OT security became a big topic.
g: IT and OT coming together on connected networks.
Total physical separation of a network from others.

quiz.q: What is OT?
o: Systems that monitor or control physical equipment
quiz.w: OT detects or causes change through direct monitoring and control of equipment and processes.

quiz.q: Which is typical OT?
o: A PLC controlling a production line
quiz.w: PLCs and SCADA are classic OT components.

quiz.q: Why did OT security become a big topic?
o: OT got connected to IT networks, ending its isolation
quiz.w: Convergence removed the protection that isolation once gave.

lessons.title: PLC, SCADA and HMI in plain words

src.l: GE Vernova: PLC, HMI and SCADA
NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: A PLC is an industrial computer built for reliability in dust, heat and vibration. It reads inputs such as sensors, runs its program, and switches outputs such as motors and valves, over and over, many times per second.
g: Signals coming into a controller from sensors, and going out to equipment.
A device that measures something, like temperature or pressure.

pages.t: An HMI is the screen where an operator sees status, alarms and trends, and can give commands such as switching off a pump. It can be a panel on the machine or a PC in a control room.
g: Human-machine interface: the operator's screen and buttons.
A warning that something needs attention.

pages.t: SCADA supervises many PLCs and remote units, often across sites far apart. It collects data, shows overview screens and records alarms. PLCs usually keep controlling even if the link to SCADA goes down.
g: Remote terminal unit: a field unit for remote sites, often using radio or mobile links.
Watch and adjust from above, rather than do the control directly.

quiz.q: What does a PLC do?
o: Controls a machine or process by reading inputs and driving outputs
quiz.w: It runs a program in a cycle: read inputs, run logic, set outputs.

quiz.q: What is an HMI?
quiz.w: HMI means human-machine interface.

quiz.q: If the link to the SCADA centre fails, what happens to the PLCs?
o: They can keep controlling their process on their own
quiz.w: PLCs and RTUs can usually keep controlling on their own if communications fail.

lessons.title: Why OT puts uptime and safety first

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: IT security traditionally centres on confidentiality, integrity and availability, often with confidentiality first: keep data secret. OT puts safety, reliability and availability first, because a failure can cause physical harm, damage or a stopped plant.
g: Keeping information secret from those who should not see it.

pages.t: In IT you can reboot a server at night and patch it weekly. In OT, machines often run continuously, and an update or restart can halt production or cause danger. Outages must often be planned days or weeks ahead, so changes are careful and often rare.
g: A software update that fixes a bug or security hole.
A period when a system is not working.

pages.t: Do not pitch OT customers like an office. Their words are uptime, safety and production. A security product must not disturb the process. Stability and predictability sell better than features.
g: The actual making of goods, which a plant must not interrupt.

quiz.q: What does OT typically prioritise?
quiz.w: OT failure can cause physical danger and downtime, so these come first.

quiz.q: Why is patching harder in OT?
o: Systems run continuously and a restart can stop production
quiz.w: Continuous operation makes restarts and updates risky.

quiz.q: A plant manager hears your pitch about advanced features. What lands better?
o: It will not disturb production and keeps the line running
quiz.w: OT buyers value stability and predictability.

lessons.title: Industrial protocols by name and purpose

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: A protocol is the language devices use to talk. Industrial equipment has its own. You do not need the details, just the names and what each is for, so you understand what a customer's network carries.
g: A set of rules for how devices exchange data.
An older name for networks that connect controllers and field devices.

pages.t: Modbus: simple, old (1979) and still widely used, but with no built-in security. PROFINET: Ethernet-based, fast and time-critical, common in factories. OPC UA: a modern standard for exchanging data from machines up to software and the cloud, with security built in.

Protocols decide whether equipment can talk to each other and what a security device must understand. Some firewalls and gateways support industrial protocols. Ask the customer which protocols they use before recommending hardware.
g: A device that translates between two networks or protocols.

quiz.q: Which protocol is known as simple, old and without built-in security?
quiz.w: Modbus is simple and widespread but provides no security against unauthorised commands.

quiz.q: What is OPC UA mainly for?
o: Standardised data exchange from machines to software and cloud
quiz.w: It is a platform-independent data exchange standard with security profiles.

quiz.q: A factory uses PROFINET. What does this tell you?
o: Their machines talk over time-critical industrial Ethernet
quiz.w: PROFINET is an Ethernet-based standard strong at tight timing.

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: The Purdue model arranges an industrial site in levels. Level 0 is the physical process, level 1 the controllers and field devices, level 2 control and HMI/SCADA, level 3 production operations, and level 4 business systems like ERP.
g: A reference model that splits industrial IT and OT into levels.
Enterprise resource planning: the company's main business software.

pages.t: Lower levels are close to the machines and must stay safe and stable. Upper levels are the business network. Grouping levels into zones lets you control what talks between them, rather than letting everything reach everything.
g: A group of systems with similar security needs.

pages.h: Why it helps in a talk
pages.t: It gives you and the customer a simple map. 'Where does your SCADA sit, and what connects it to the office?' Real sites are messier than the model, so treat it as a concept for discussion, not a rule.
g: A simplified picture used to discuss real systems.

quiz.q: Where do ERP and business systems sit in the Purdue model?
quiz.w: Business logistics systems like ERP sit at the top, level 4.

quiz.q: Which levels are closest to the physical process?
quiz.w: Level 0 is the process itself, level 1 the controlling devices.

quiz.q: Why group systems into zones?
o: To control what traffic passes between groups
quiz.w: Zones with controlled links limit what can reach sensitive systems.

lessons.title: Industrial hardware: DIN rail, wide temperature, redundancy

src.l: Cisco ISA 3000 data sheet (DIN rail industrial firewall)

pages.t: Industrial gear is mounted on a DIN rail, a standard 35 mm metal rail inside control cabinets. Switches, routers and firewalls for factories often clip onto it, instead of sitting on a desk or in a 19 inch rack.
g: A standard metal rail for mounting devices in cabinets.
A metal enclosure holding the electrical and control equipment.

pages.t: Factory equipment must cope with temperature extremes, humidity, dust and vibration, so industrial devices are made rugged, with wide temperature ratings and robust connectors. Fibre links also avoid electrical noise.
g: A rating for working in both very cold and very hot places.
Optical cable that carries light and is not affected by electrical noise.

pages.t: Interruptions are costly, so industrial networks use redundancy: ring layouts, dual power inputs and spare paths, so one failure does not stop production. Ask whether the customer needs a spare path or power.
g: Having a spare path, power input or device ready to take over.
A cable loop where traffic can go either way round if one link breaks.

quiz.q: What is a DIN rail?
o: A standard rail inside cabinets to mount devices
quiz.w: It is a standardised metal mounting rail in control cabinets.

quiz.q: Why do industrial devices have wide temperature ratings?
o: Factories and outdoor cabinets can be very hot or cold
quiz.w: Industrial sites include temperature extremes, humidity and vibration.

quiz.q: A customer says one failed switch must never stop production. What do you discuss?
o: Redundancy such as a ring or dual power
quiz.w: Spare paths and power prevent a single failure from stopping production.

lessons.title: Segmentation and the firewall between IT and OT

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security
Cisco ISA 3000 data sheet (DIN rail industrial firewall)

pages.t: Segmentation splits a network into smaller parts. If an intruder gets into one part, it is harder to move on to the rest, and a local fault stays local. Firewalls and VLANs are the usual tools.
g: Dividing a network into separate parts with controlled links.
A virtual separate network on shared hardware.

pages.t: Many OT systems are long-lived, hard to patch and use protocols with no authentication. Connecting office and plant opens risk. A firewall between IT and OT lets only the traffic you allow through and shields weak devices.
g: A device that allows or blocks network traffic by rules.

pages.t: Good designs also split OT into zones, such as one production line per zone, so a problem cannot spread across the plant. Industrial firewalls often mount on a DIN rail and some understand industrial protocols.
g: A firewall built for plant conditions and OT protocols.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of segmentation?
o: It limits how far an intruder or fault can spread
It removes the need for passwords
quiz.w: Splitting the network contains breaches and local failures.

quiz.q: Why put a firewall between IT and OT?
o: Allow only needed traffic and protect fragile OT devices
quiz.w: Many OT devices are hard to patch, so controlled access in front of them matters.

quiz.q: A customer has one flat network with the office and the production line. Best first suggestion?
o: Separate them with a firewall and zones
quiz.w: A firewall between IT and OT is a common first step, and NIST names firewalls as the main way to protect OT devices.

lessons.title: IEC 62443 and NIS2 at a glance

src.l: NCSC Ireland NIS2 quick reference guide

pages.t: ISA/IEC 62443 is a series of standards for securing industrial automation and control systems. It covers asset owners, product suppliers, system integrators and service providers, and builds on shared responsibility between them.
g: A company that designs and builds a solution from many products for a customer.

pages.t: NIS2 is an EU directive on cybersecurity covering 18 sectors. Highly critical ones include energy, transport, health and water. Others include manufacturing of certain products. Medium and large companies in these sectors must manage cyber risk and report significant incidents.
g: An EU law that each country turns into national law.
A security event that disrupts or threatens operations.

pages.h: What to say in a sales talk
pages.t: NIS2 is one reason many customers now ask about OT security, and 62443 is a recognised yardstick for products and projects. You are not a lawyer: say it is a topic, and ask whether they know if they are covered.
g: A company that falls under the rules of a law.

quiz.q: Who does IEC 62443 address?
o: Asset owners, suppliers, integrators and service providers
quiz.w: The series defines requirements for these four stakeholder groups.

quiz.q: What does NIS2 require of covered companies at a high level?
o: Manage cybersecurity risk and report significant incidents
quiz.w: Risk-management measures and incident reporting are core obligations.

quiz.q: A customer asks 'Does NIS2 apply to us?' What is a good answer?
o: It depends on sector and size, so check with your adviser or authority
quiz.w: Coverage depends on sector and size, and legal advice is not our role.

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: Typical OT sites: manufacturing, power and utilities, water and wastewater, oil and gas, mining, and transport. Buildings also run OT, for example for HVAC and access control.
g: A company supplying power, water or similar services.

pages.t: Resellers in OT are often system integrators, machine builders and electrical contractors. They think in projects and cabinets, and value products that fit their standards. The end user, such as a plant, often sets the rules.
g: A company that makes industrial machines and often installs the control system.

pages.t: Many OT sites are small and remote, such as pumping stations. They need rugged routers, remote access and monitoring. Cellular routers and small industrial firewalls are often a good fit.
g: Securely connecting to a site from far away to monitor or fix it.

quiz.q: Which is a typical OT environment?
quiz.w: Water, power, oil and gas and manufacturing are classic OT sectors.

quiz.q: Who is the typical reseller in OT?
quiz.w: Integrators and machine builders deliver OT projects.

quiz.q: A remote pumping station needs monitoring. Which hardware kind fits?
quiz.w: Remote sites call for rugged, remote-manageable connectivity.

src.l: NIST SP 800-82r3 Guide to OT security

pages.t: OT projects are slower: design, testing, a planned stop for installation. Customers often prefer products that are proven. Lifecycle matters: equipment may stay for ten years or more, so long availability and support count.
g: The time a product is on sale and supported.

pages.t: Speak about uptime, safety and production, not 'threats'. Good questions: What must never stop? Which protocols and PLCs do you use? Who owns OT, IT or the plant? Is remote access needed?
g: A person or team with an interest in or say over a project.

pages.t: IT and OT teams often disagree: IT wants patching and control, OT wants nothing to change. A successful pitch respects both: protects the plant without disturbing production, and gives IT visibility.
g: Being able to see what is on the network and what it does.

quiz.q: Why does lifecycle matter more in OT?
o: Equipment may stay in place for many years
quiz.w: Long service life makes long availability and support important.

quiz.q: Which opening question suits an OT customer?
o: How many laptops do you have?
quiz.w: It speaks their language of uptime and production.

quiz.q: IT wants frequent updates, OT wants nothing to change. What do you do?
o: Offer protection that does not disturb production and gives IT visibility
quiz.w: Respecting both concerns builds trust.
